bugs: $disk->delete() is not wrapped in try/catch (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:82). If the disk config ever sets throw=true or a driver throws, the run aborts after earlier chunks were already deleted, and the remaining rows are never attempted. Minor, because the configured local disk has throw=false and returns false.
antipatterns: The fixed 7200s lock TTL has no relation to how long the run takes. If a run on millions of rows takes longer than that, the lock expires and a second run can overlap (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:23,47)
The schedule has no withoutOverlapping() and relies only on the command's own lock. That works, but it isn't stated in the schedule definition (routes/console.php:11)
The interactive-confirmation tests need #[RunInSeparateProcess] to get Prompts to ask, which is a heavy workaround (tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:123,133)
strengths: Uses ConfirmableTrait, so production confirmation and --force work the standard Laravel way, and a declined prompt returns FAILURE
chunkById plus partition() deletes each chunk's rows in one whereKey()->delete() query. Kept rows don't break id-based paging. This is memory-safe and fast on millions of rows
Rejects --days below 1 (FILTER_VALIDATE_INT with min_range 1) and returns INVALID, so --days=0 can't wipe the whole table by accident
Dry-run runs before the confirmation and the lock and only counts rows
A Cache::lock released in finally keeps manual and scheduled runs from overlapping; the schedule uses onOneServer on shared Redis

The most thorough tests: interactive yes and no, --no-interaction refusal, a failure partway through the run, retry on the next run, a chunk boundary of 501, invalid days, lock held and lock released, schedule, and disk config
Index on created_at, a #[Scope] attribute, and a createdAt factory state

bugs: --days=0 is accepted ('non-negative'). It purges every export created before this second; my probe confirmed a 1-minute-old export was deleted. That is a dangerous footgun on a production purge (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:23)
antipatterns: Writes its own operatorApproves() with isProduction()/force/confirm() instead of using the framework's ConfirmableTrait (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:68-75)
Deletes one row per query with $export->delete() inside lazyById. On millions of rows that is one query per row instead of a batch delete per chunk (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:86-95)
Invalid --days returns FAILURE instead of INVALID (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:26)
Has both withoutOverlapping() and the command's own Cache::lock, so the overlap protection is duplicated (routes/console.php:11-14)
strengths: The only implementation that wraps disk deletes in try/catch, calls report(), and counts thrown exceptions as failures, so the run continues and exits with a failure code
Holds a 6h command lock released in finally, plus onOneServer and withoutOverlapping on the schedule. This is the most robust protection against overlap
lazyById(1000) is memory-safe, and the created_at index is present
Tests cover interactive yes and no without a separate process, force, a thrown delete exception, a delete that returns false, a chunk boundary, the lock, and the schedule including withoutOverlapping
Partial Mockery mocks of the real disk keep the failure tests realistic

bugs: --days=0 is accepted (min_range 0). It purges every export, including ones just created; my probe confirmed this (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:23)

The lock TTL is only 3600s while rows are deleted one query at a time. On a few million rows the run can take longer than an hour, the lock expires, and a scheduled run can overlap a manual one. The schedule has no withoutOverlapping() to cover this (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:43, routes/console.php:11-14)
antipatterns: Hardcodes ->timezone('Europe/Copenhagen'), which the task didn't ask for (routes/console.php:13)

Failure tests replace the disk by setting Storage::shouldReceive('disk') to return an ad-hoc anonymous class that doesn't implement Filesystem. The test only works because nothing else touches the facade (tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:148-162,177-185)

The production refusal test has no expectsConfirmation. It passes only because Prompts is non-interactive under the test harness, and the confirm-yes path is never tested (tests/Feature/PurgeExportsTest.php:121-130)
Deletes one row per query with $export->delete() (app/Console/Commands/PurgeExports.php:81)
strengths: Uses ConfirmableTrait for the production confirmation, with --force for unattended runs
Catches Throwable on file delete, calls report(), and counts it as a failure, so the run continues
Returns INVALID for a bad --days value
The command lock is released in finally, and the schedule uses onOneServer
Tests include a chunk boundary of 1100 rows and both a thrown delete and a delete that returns false

v.rationale: I ran the tests and read every added file for all three implementations. All three suites pass: impl-1 20 tests, impl-2 17, impl-3 18. In each implementation I probed a real permission-denied file on the local disk, and all three keep the row and exit with a failure code. impl-1 ranks first. It uses the framework's ConfirmableTrait and deletes in batches with chunkById plus partition, issuing one delete query per chunk, which is the most efficient approach on millions of rows. It rejects --days=0 and has the most complete tests, including retry on the next run and the interactive prompt. Its weaknesses are small: file deletes aren't wrapped in try/catch, which matters little because the disk has throw=false, and it uses a fixed 2h lock. impl-2 ranks second. It handles thrown delete exceptions, and its overlap protection is the strongest: a 6h lock plus withoutOverlapping. Its tests test the interactive prompt in-process. Against that, it writes its own confirmation instead of using ConfirmableTrait, deletes one row per query, and accepts --days=0, which purges everything. impl-3 ranks third. It is idiomatic in the command, using ConfirmableTrait, select plus lazyById, and catching delete failures. But it combines a 1h lock TTL with per-row deletes, so a long run on millions of rows can lose the lock and overlap. It also accepts --days=0, hardcodes a timezone nobody asked for, and its tests are weaker: hacky anonymous-class disk mocks, and a refusal test that never checks the prompt.
